speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE INQUIRY AS TO ATTENDANCE OF PREMIER OF QUEBEC AND COMMENTS ON AGENDA
speechtext:
That question, put in that form, completely misrepresents the scope, purpose and effect of this conference. This, Mr. Speaker, in the view of the government is a very important conference, and the importance which the government attaches to it is reflected in the preparations that have been made for it and in the broad and comprehensive scope of the matters that are to come before it.
As I have endeavoured to indicate on previous occasions, one of the difficulties that have beset the plenary dominion-provincial conferences in the past has been that each side, the dominion government on the one hand and the provinces on the other, has come to the conference with preconceived ideas and positions. There has not been a comprehensive study of the whole tax structure of this country so far as it affects both the dominion and the provinces.
This has been badly needed and it has been badly needed not simply on the basis of a dominion study but on the basis of a co-operative study. We have a federal system in this country under which provincial governments are sovereign. They have their rights; they have their powers, and they have heavy responsibilities. The federal government has its powers, its rights and its heavy responsibilities as well. The view of the government has been that if we are going to do anything effective on a long-term basis in this country to help governments at all levels to work effectively together in relation to fiscal problems, there must be a comprehensive study, and it must be undertaken on a co-operative basis.
It is our hope, Mr. Speaker, that at this conference we will be able to bring about something that has not been effectively done

Inquiries of the Ministry before in the realm of dominion-provincial fiscal relations in this country; in other words, a comprehensive co-operative study of those common problems with a view to achieving long range comprehensive understandings and arrangements in regard to them.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, just before the house rose last night the Leader of the Opposition asked for some information regarding the procedures which had been followed to enable the government to reach a decision as to the plane which would be selected to re-equip certain squadrons of the air division of the R.C.A.F. in Europe. I explained briefly last night the procedure and the methods which had been followed. I should like to repeat that today and elaborate a little so as to give the Leader of the Opposition all the information I have at my disposal.
It will be recalled that the F-86 had been in operation in Europe for some time, and it was therefore becoming obvious that sooner

or later this aircraft would have to be replaced. About a year and a half ago a committee of experts in the R.C.A.F. was set up to investigate the various alternative planes which were then in existence or which were even on the drawing boards at that time.
That committee of experts has been carrying out examinations ever since that date. It has been a continuous exercise in which every possible endeavour has been made to ascertain the most suitable aircraft to be employed by the air force. Of course a final decision could not be reached until early this year, when the exact role which the air force would be required to carry out in Europe became clearer.
The committee of experts repeatedly reported to the chief of the air staff, who kept personally conversant with every examination and test made. The chief of the air staff kept me informed periodically as these examinations and evaluations were continued. He also kept the chiefs of staff committee informed of their progress.
Gradually certain types of aircraft were eliminated by the R.C.A.F. because they did not meet the operational requirements which were set out. All examinations made by the R.C.A.F. experts were based purely on military and operational grounds. As the R.C.A.F. was reaching a conclusion, meetings of the chiefs of staff were held almost daily on this matter so there could be combined recommendations made by the chiefs of staff committee.
Subsequently those recommendations were submitted to the cabinet defence committee. When they were submitted to the cabinet defence committee, and in fact before they had been submitted, the closest touch was maintained with the officials of the Department of Defence Production; and while the recommendations from my department were based entirely on military and operational grounds, the Department of Defence Production officials also took into consideration the various matters connected with the production of these types of aircraft, the way in which they could be produced here in Canada, and went into details regarding costs, etc., of the different types which were under examination. Finally, after the cabinet defence committee was prepared to make a recommendation to cabinet as a whole, the matter was considered by cabinet as a whole.
It might be of some interest to hon. members opposite to know some of the types of aircraft which were examined. I will just mention a few of them. Actually nearly 20 or more types of aircraft were given an examination of some kind or another, but

some of the principal ones which were given an exhaustive examination were the F-102 Convair, the F11-1F Super Tiger Grumman, the Blackburn NA-39 and the Blackburn 109, the Northrop 156, the McDonnell F-4H and the McDonnell F-101C, the Lockheed 104, the French Mirage made by Marcel Dassault, the Republic 105, the A-IIIJ North American and the CF-100 and F-86 to see whether they could be converted to the role.
Among the criteria which were set out in order to enable a just assessment to be made was suitability to the role which was given to us when General Norstad visited Ottawa a few weeks ago. Of course the serviceability of the aircraft had to be given high consideration, and the availability; when could this aircraft come into service? Then on the economic side, the cost and the amount of work which might be provided in Canada had to be considered. Could these planes be manufactured under licence or would they have to be bought outright? There was the question of production sharing, how much work could be carried out in Canada on other projects which were being carried out by some of these companies. Would they share the production with our own industry in making parts for some of the aircraft which might be used by the United States air force or by civilian operations?
In fact I can say that the decision was based on military, operational and economic grounds. A question was asked yesterday, could not a larger type of aircraft-mind you, the size of the aircraft governs the cost -have been used in fewer numbers than a smaller aircraft which would, for each copy, cost less than a larger one? It was emphatically stated that from the military and operational requirements point of view those requirements could not be met with a fewer number of aircraft. In fact, for a strike reconnaissance role rather small aircraft are preferred.
I believe this gives some indication of the extended and exhaustive studies which were made. Yesterday we were told we should have reached this decision months ago. Why was this decision not taken last December? No sooner had we been accused of being dilatory in that respect than we were told we had selected the wrong aircraft. I can assure hon. members that this government does not apologize for having taken considerable time to make a thorough examination so as to be certain that the taxpayers' money was being spent to the best advantage. As a result of this prolonged examination the cabinet did come to the conclusion that they would reequip the air division with the Lockheed
Supply-National Defence 104G, the "G" being the mark of that particular series or family of aircraft. I am satisfied that the taxpayers' money is being spent to the best advantage by the purchase of this particular aircraft.
This is a proven aricraft. It is supersonic. It is a small aircraft with a very high performance. It can also be refueled in the air, so it could be deployed in Europe or in any other part of the world in order to carry out its strike reconnaissance role. There are various types of this family of aircraft already in operation. They are in operation with the United States air force on this continent, in Europe, in Turkey and in the Far East. I emphasize the fact that they are in operation in Europe and the commander in chief of the European forces, General Norstad, has expressed satisfaction with this type of aircraft, and has indicated to this government that the re-equipment of the air division squadrons with the "G" variety of the 104 will be entirely acceptable to him.
The other day in speaking here I mentioned that it has been noted that the Federal Republic of Germany is also re-equipping its squadrons, which today are equipped with the same aircraft as our squadrons, the F-86, with this F-104G for a strike reconnaissance role. As a matter of fact we have been in close consultation with the Germans for a number of months on this matter. We have had teams of the R.C.A.F. in Europe in order to find out how the independent assessment made by the Germans was progressing, and which aircraft they were going to accept. It would be interesting, I think, to hon. members to learn that as late as March 31 a contract was signed between the government of the Federal Republic of Germany and the company concerned for the acquisition of a number of these aircraft. Even more recently, only last week, we had officers of the R.C.A.F. in Paris conferring with their German colleagues, and the latter expressed satisfaction that the German air force had in this particular aircraft.
Now, of course, the advocates of other types of aircraft will naturally belittle the type which has been successful. An unsucces-ful competitor will naturally feel disappointed that he has not received an order. I might say that for months I have been subjected, as have the officers of the R.C.A.F. and the Minister of Defence Production, to daily visits from the representatives of these various companies. They have enlarged upon the benefits of their own particular aircraft. I have at all times endeavoured to take a detached point of view in order not to be prejudiced in favour of one or the other type of aircraft. I have listened patiently to all their representations. These have been recorded; they have been examined again and

Supply-National Defence again by the officials of my department and the officials of the Department of Defence Production.
I must say some of the statements made by the hon. member for Trinity yesterday were exactly the same as some of the statements which have been made in my office. But we had the facilities for testing the accuracy of those statements, and they have been tested.

You can take your choice. These are all good

planes. They have certain characteristics which are or are not capable of meeting the military requirements or the economic requirements. These have, as I say, been thoroughly examined and tested during the past few months.
We have also considered how quickly pilots who were accustomed to operating the F-86 could be trained to operate a new plane which was acceptable. That has been shown, and our pilots have already flown the F-104, not the 104-G but the other models of this aircraft. They have already flown it and they have demonstrated their ability to change very quickly from flying the Sabre jet, the F-86, to flying the 104.
With respect to some of the utterly erroneous, exaggerated and irresponsible statements made by the hon. member for Trinity, I would like to call attention to some of these facts. He says this aircraft was grounded two years ago. Has not practically every aircraft which is in operation today been grounded at some time or other? I recall that the Comet II was grounded a number of years ago for a very long period. Is the hon. member going to stand up and say that the Comet IV of today, which is regarded as the best aircraft of its type anywhere in the world, because a previous mark or type of that aircraft was grounded a few years ago, is of no ruddy use?

speechtext: Of course you did.

Then the hon. member went on discussing at considerable length the qualities of the original 104. The original 104 was designed, as he said correctly, for the purpose of aerial combat. It attained great distinction in being able to fly at great height, and was regarded as one of the superior aircraft of that period for its particular mission at that time. But that is not the plane we are getting. We are getting the advanced edition of that particular family of aircraft, one which is having special characteristics introduced into its

framework and over-all picture in order that it can carry out the attack reconnaissance plan.
The hon. member did say that the faults which had been discovered during the period of development and in the early operational stages have now been corrected. We are taking advantage of the fact that this aircraft has been proved. We are not in the position of having to pay large sums of money for the development of this aircraft, or to wait for a number of years until it has been thoroughly tested. It is a tested and proven aircraft, stable in frame and absolutely operational, sound for the role for which it is designed.
Then the hon. member referred to the fatality rate and the accident rate. In my office I heard the same figures quoted that the hon. member mentioned, and then I call attention to the fact that fatality and accident rates are never released by any government. We never release any fatality percentages or rates, nor does the United States. These were figures which were given-

whether he has read the hearings before the congressional defence committee on this particular point of fatality rates?

speechtext:
I can say without any fear of contradiction by anybody who has the facts that the accident rate, even in the early days of the first 104, was not abnormal. You cannot
Supply-National Defence fly aircraft without having casualties; there are bound to be casualties, but it is quite wrong to suggest that this aircraft is not airworthy and has any higher accident rate than other aircraft. Therefore I repeat, the statements which were made last night were inaccurate, they were misleading and were stated without any real sense of responsibility. They are purely hearsay evidence by prejudiced personnel.
In closing, I do not think I can do better than refer to a very well-known book, which I am sure all hon. members here have read. I refer to "Pilgrim's Progress". It may be remembered that when Mr. Valiant for Truth was nearly reaching the celestial city he met three men, one of whose name was Wildhead, who approached him and endeavoured to persuade him not to proceed by telling him of the terrible dangers and difficulties which he exaggerated, and he urged him to turn back. Then you will probably recall that Mr. Valiant for Truth remarked about this adventure in these words:
Who so beset him round
With dismal stories,
Do but themselves confound.
I think the dismal stories which were advanced last night by the hon. member for Trinity have utterly confounded him in the eyes of all those who know what they are talking about.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the minister no doubt thinks that by his quotation from "Pilgrim's Progress" he has knocked the stuffing out of our case, that perhaps some questioning in regard to this decision of the government is required. We on this side do not question the detachment or the desire of the minister to make the right decision, and we do not question his right to insist that this was the right decision and was the best plane; that the other planes were inferior and this was the right one. Therefore I should think he would want to show us the same consideration when we do question the possibility of this being the right decision. It is our duty and it is our right to criticize him, and I hope we can do so without the minister imputing motives to us of the kind he has already suggested.
We will have a good many questions to ask the minister, and by his replies he may be able to show that this is undoubtedly the best plane, the most economical plane and the best in every way; but we are going to ask him these questions and we will expect the detailed information in reply to those questions which will, at least in his view, confirm the decision he has made.
Before we begin to ask these questions of detail regarding capability, performance and

Supply-National Defence all that kind of thing, I would like to make some more general observations and ask him some more general questions which will provide the foundation, I hope, for the subsequent questions. I would ask the minister if he could explain in some detail, because it is a very important matter, the nature of the new role that is now being undertaken by part of the Canadian air division attached to the NATO forces in Europe. It is a new role; it is bound to be a difficult role, a role of responsibility. Perhaps it is a new departure in our participation in NATO military activity in Europe, and I think the committee would like to know something about it.
The minister has called it a strike reconnaissance role. He has also, I think, referred to it, or it has been referred to, as a strike attack role. We would like to know exactly what this change involves as far as the remaining squadrons-I think four CF-100 squadrons, although I may be wrong in that figure-are concerned. The minister said last night that they will continue the role they have been performing in Europe. Perhaps the minister will explain to us how they will be able to carry out that role in the future. They will no doubt be functionally detached from the new squadrons and will be carrying out the old role in new conditions of capability of attack. But we are more interested at the moment in the picture of the new strike attack or new strike reconnaissance role and what it involves for the R.C.A.F.
We are also interested, as I know the committee will be, in the conditions under which this new NATO role will have to be carried out. I understand, and the minister will correct me if I am wrong, that the headquarters of six of the twelve R.C.A.F. squadrons are located in France; the others are in Germany. I believe it is the case, and again the minister will correct me if I am wrong, that France has not seen fit to integrate her own air forces with the NATO forces under NATO command. Also, France in the exercise of her sovereign rights has not found it possible to facilitate certain plans of the United States as part of European NATO forces for the storage and use of nuclear weapons which the United States consider to be an indispensable part of the NATO forces and which indeed, as was pointed out yesterday, General Norstad has said is the capability on which all NATO planning and tactics are now based.
As a result of this stand taken at the present time by France-perhaps France may reverse her decision-the United States air forces contemplate leaving the NATO air fields in France for other sites where these difficulties will not be encountered. Therefore


the minister might tell the committee in some greater detail than he did when I asked him a question about this the other day what will happen if the United States feels it must make that decision. I suppose the result would be that the only foreign squadrons-by "foreign" I mean non-French squadrons- left in France would be those of the R.C.A.F. I believe it is also true that at the present time the Canadian air units depend for their logistics and their supply on the United States military pipe line. They get their ammunition, their aviation fuel and their rations through that United States pipe line.
Therefore I ask, because I think the question is particularly pertinent at this time when we are contemplating the re-equipment of Canadian air squadrons in France, how these squadrons could be maintained economically if all this was cut off, quite apart from the fact, although this is not strictly relevant to this particular question but perhaps I might mention it, that this whole system of NATO infrastructure will be very seriously affected, communications, the oil pipe line and all the rest of it, if the United States squadrons feel that they have to leave France. Surely this is an important thing to know before we discuss in detail the nature of the decision reached by the government to re-equip these squadrons, and perhaps the minister would be good enough at this time to deal with these two somewhat background subjects.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
First of all, dealing with the new role, it is that of strike reconnaissance. I explained in some detail when I was speaking the day before yesterday what that role was. I pointed out how the Russian ground troops are in considerable numbers along the Russian border and in satellite countries. If the Russians started a war those troops would very likely move through to overrun the countries of western Europe.
It is desirable in the first place to have reconnaissance aircraft which are fast and able to get information as to the movement of columns so those columns can be engaged either by those aircraft or by other means at the disposal of the commander; for instance, by missiles such as the Lacrosse which we will have in our own brigades in the not far distant future. I think that is a fairly obvious role. It is necessary to have this reconnaissance work carried out; and it is essential, now that the means of engaging aircraft have been made more effective, that these planes be small and fast.
In addition there might be targets of opportunity. One might find that there would be a moving column of armoured fighting vehicles. It would be difficult to attack such

a column with missiles because it would be moving; it would be much easier to use missiles against ground and stationary targets such as airfields. So in addition to the reconnaissance role which would be performed by this aircraft it would also have the power to attack targets of opportunity as they arose.
If we were to go one step further and take a longer view, this is all part of the contribution to the deterrent which makes it quite obvious to the Russians that it is not worth while launching their attack through western Europe because we have the means of locating and attacking their columns if they advance; and if we are equipped with the latest weapons of attack, the destruction to advancing columns might be very, very heavy. So it is as part of our western deterrent, part of our endeavour to preserve the peace, that we are equipping these aircraft and having them prepared for this new role.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Before the minister leaves that point, may I ask him whether it is part of his argument-and I think he has just said this; perhaps he would elaborate on it-that missiles are less effective against moving targets than this type of strike reconnaissance plane?

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
I think my words were that it might be more difficult for missiles to attack a moving target. Obviously there is more flexibility with aircraft than there is with a missile in its present state of development, when it is designed as a ground to ground weapon.
Regarding the maintenance of the squadrons which are in France, it is perfectly correct that at the present time we have the headquarters of the air division and six squadrons located on French soil. The other six squadrons are located on German soil. There are alternate air fields selected for these squadrons so that in a period of operations or in an emergency these squadrons could be moved to a different air field. It would not be a very difficult matter if it were found necessary, in the hypothetical situation which the Leader of the Opposition presented, to move the six squadrons which are in France to German air fields and double up there or occupy other alternate fields; or it might be necessary to move them somewhere else.
So far as we know at the present time however, it would be the intention of the Americans to maintain their pipe line to their French bases. The bases will probably remain, and there are other aircraft of the United States air force in France which would not be equipped with nuclear weapons. So
Supply-National Defence that at the present time, while we are looking into the various possibilities and thinking about this matter, no firm decision has been reached as to what would be necessary, and it is not necessary to make a firm decision until we know exactly what course will be taken by the French government and by the United States.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Perhaps I might complete that part of my question by saying I devoutly hope, as I am sure the minister does, that this contingency will never arise and that the French and United States governments may be able to solve their difficulties with regard to this important problem of the control of NATO atomic weapons. But I assume that if the difficulty does arise and the United States has to make arrangements to take most of its squadrons out of France, the Canadian squadrons could if necessary, be moved to other air fields; or, if they were kept in France, they would still be on a United States pipe line even though it might be a little more difficult and expensive than the present arrangement.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: That is correct. No decision has been reached, nor could it be reached, to move them at the present time. I think it would be most undesirable to move them now, because I share the hope expressed by the Leader of the Opposition that the two governments principally concerned will be able to reach a satisfactory agreement.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: I wonder if the minister would be good enough to let the committee know whether the Lockheed F-104 was in fact the plane he recommended as his selection to the cabinet defence committee.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I cannot disclose, and I do not intend to disclose, the discussions which took place in the cabinet defence committee, and I am not going to say whether I recommended it or whether anybody else recommended another plane. The matter was thoroughly discussed, and on military, operational and economic grounds the selection was made. It was a cabinet decision. Naturally all members of the cabinet thoroughly endorsed that decision.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: May I ask the minister whether the chiefs of staff recommended more than one plane to the cabinet defence committee.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
The chiefs of staff made an appraisal of the value of several planes, and the pros and cons were considered by them with respect to each of the different types and they made a recommendation.

Supply-National Defence

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Could the minister tell us if in that evaluation the chiefs of staff gave a priority on the basis of their rating?

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: I think it is a time-honoured policy which has been followed by this and the preceding government that the recommendations of the servants of the government are not disclosed in public. I do not think it is right to ask me to say whether the chiefs of staff recommended this or that plane. If I were to say today that the chiefs of staff did recommend a certain plane it may be that at some future time the government would have to take a decision which was not entirely compatible with the recommendations of the chiefs of staff. The opposition would then say, "Well, you did say that the chiefs of staff made this recommendation," and we might be in a difficult position. I say that the military and economic information was placed before the cabinet and that the decision of the government was based on military and economic grounds.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I did not ask the minister to tell me which plane the chiefs of staff committee recommended. I merely asked if they had given a priority, one over the other, on the basis of their evaluation. It may be a time-honoured custom not to make public the recommendations of governmental advisors, and that is probably an excellent principle which has long been held, but it is an equally time-honoured and a most important proviso that ministers of the crown, when asking for sums of money from the public purse in such astronomical amounts as $1.7 billion, should give this committee enough information on which to make an intelligent decision. That the minister is not doing.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: I am quite prepared to go this far. I can tell the committee that the chiefs of staff did make a firm recommendation for a certain plane.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the minister has laid down a principle to which I certainly take no exception; that civil servants, whether they are military or civil, should not be brought into parliamentary discussions as justification for any action of the government one way or the other. That is a principle which has not been invariably observed in the last year or so. I would mention to the minister that earlier in this session the Prime Minister quoted a recommendation, or an approval or decision, of the chiefs of staff as justification for certain actions being taken by the government.

speechtext:

each of the following planes was flown by R.C.A.F. pilots for evaluation purposes. Perhaps the minister would like to make a note of the planes:

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Obviously, Mr. Chairman, I would not have that information readily available, and it will have to be acquired.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the minister said that one consideration-and I am sure it was an important one in the minds of the government in this decision-was the availability of the aircraft in question. subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman, some could have been purchased outright.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: These are technical details which are considered classified regarding aircraft, and it is unreasonable to expect me to disclose here in public all the technical details regarding aircraft we are acquiring in order, if necessary, to fight the battle for the defence of Canada and of the west. Surely if we give all these technical details to a potential enemy his task is simplified. I do not think I should be called upon to answer such questions.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I understand that the NATO military authorities had what I could perhaps call a competition, though that may not be exactly the right word, to decide on a suitable strike fighter for NATO use in what was, I think, a most praiseworthy effort to agree that there should be one plane for this purpose only, and that as a result of this examination or competition, or whatever you wish to call it, the NATO military authorities chose a Fiat designed strike fighter as the best developed yet for this purpose.
I believe the minister said this plane was considered. If it was, would he tell us what efforts were made to test its capabilities and why, when it was considered by NATO as the best strike fighter designed for that purpose, it was not possible to go along with that decision? There were United States planes considered by NATO at that time when agreement was sought to be reached in NATO concerning the best strike fighter available for NATO use.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman, efforts have been made over many years to standardize the various types of equipment which are used by our NATO partners. No one can claim that those efforts have been very successful. There are conflicts between the different nations, making it extremely difficult for one type of equipment to be accepted by all nations.
The type of aircraft to which the Leader of the Opposition referred was the G-91. That was an aircraft for the direct support of troops. It had a role different from that which is being given to the squadrons of the R.C.A.F. in their strike reconnaissance. It was designed for direct tactical support of ground troops.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Perhaps this is a matter of semantics, but this plane is always referred to as a strike fighter. We talk about the present F-104 as a strike fighter and reconnaissance plane. I take it then that the roles of these two planes are quite different in the NATO organization?

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: That is my understanding. They have two different roles.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: In order to confirm the statement I made earlier I wish to say this. Here is an article which appeared on May 14, 1959 in the Globe and Mail, a newspaper which is not usually unfriendly to Conservative governments. The article refers to a visit here by General Norstad, the supreme commander in Europe of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. There is mention of

Supply-National Defence a luncheon in Toronto and then of the decisions which the government would have to make. It says these are:
1.	Whether to equip the Canadian brigade group in Europe with nuclear weapons.
2.	Whether to change the role of the R.C.A.F. squadrons in Europe from interception to that of strike attack and tactical ground support. This would mean re-equipping most or all of the 12 squadrons with between 200 and 300 new strike attack aircraft, at a cost ranging between $200 million and $400 million.
Of the two issues, the future of the air division in Europe is considered the more pressing largely because a negative decision on the part of the government would virtually put the R.C.A.F. out of business in a few years time.
The article goes on to say:
R.C.A.F. evaluation teams have been visiting aircraft plants in the United States and Britain since last fall in a search for an aircraft to replace the Sabre in Europe. Recommendations were submitted to the government about two months ago, listing at least three aircraft in order of R.C.A.F. preference:
1.	The Grumman F11F, or Super Tiger, to be produced by the Grumman Aircraft Company at Long Island, N.Y. This is a low-level attack aircraft, originally designed for aircraft carrier use, which could be modified to carry the radar needed for high level interception work as well.
2.	The Blackburn NA-39, a naval aircraft built by the Blackburn and General Aircraft Company in Yorkshire, England. R.C.A.F. reservations about this aeroplane are understood to be that it is somewhat slower than its competitors.

The article continues, Mr. Chairman, but there is no mention whatever of the F-104 Lockheed day fighter and air superiority fighter. And here we have just received confirmation from the minister that what the Germans want is a redesigned F-104. After all we have heard about this country not being in a position to develop a new weapon system we embark on another program of redesigning which will enable an aircraft not designed to do strike reconnaissance work to do the job which it was not designed to do.
The important thing about strike reconnaissance is not its ability to get to 50,000 feet fast. I should like to quote from Aviation Week of June 29 in further illustration of the German requirements in this matter:
General Brohon, who said It was Impossible for France to expend the capital outlay needed to do the job, also called on the U.S. to provide his divis-sion in particular, and France in general, with an effective replacement aircraft to carry out the division's primary mission-reconnaissance. He would like most, he said, to see a reconnaissance version of the Lockheed F-104 developed by the U.S. and supplied to him under mutual security funds. Without such a replacement for the Republic RF-84F aircraft within the next two years, he added, his division would represent a "waste of human capital" rather than an effective combat force.
There are some other interesting observations in this magazine. For example:
Paris-Spectacular demonstration by the Swedish Saab Draken and some inspired flying by French and British acrobatic teams saved this 23rd international aeronautical salon from being just another air show.
Then it goes on:
Biggest disappointment was the Lockheed F-104B demonstration, flown by Lt. Col. James Jabara. The plane made only a takeoff, a single flyby and a landing.
The minister went on to talk about availability, and subsequently he told the committee in reply to a question by the Leader of the Opposition that other aircraft were equally available. And then he gave us the same kind of mixed assurance as we were
Supply-National Defence given earlier when the Avro Arrow decision was made. He said the decision was based on a combination of factors-on cost, on what work would be done in Canada, on the military value, on the degree to which Canadians could participate in production-sharing, and so on. We know these are important, Mr. Chairman, but surely if we can afford to do anything at all in defence matters we should do it well. As the minister said, other production-sharing arrangements were available to us. If I may, I should like to quote from the Toronto Telegram dated May 14, which reads as follows:
Ottawa	(Special)-The federal government's
choice of an aircraft to replace the F-86 Sabres for the Canadian air division abroad is between the Blackburn NA-39 and Republic's new strike attack interceptor, the 105-D Thunderchief . . . The choice has been narrowed to the Blackburn or Republic planes because the advantages of Canadian production of either of these are overwhelming as compared to others.
The article goes on to say:
Should the Blackburn aircraft be chosen Prime Minister John Diefenbaker could then implement in a dramatic way his "Commonwealth policy" expressed so forcibly last fall in his Albert Hall speech in London.
And the article ends as follows:
In meetings between the Prime Minister and Mundy Peel, president of the Republic Corporation, and John S. D. Tory, Q.C., vice-president of A. V. Roe Canada Limited, the Republic Corporation undertook that Canadian-made parts would be included in the American plane for the U.S. Air Force squadrons.
The planes for Canadian use would be the same as to air-frame but would be powered by the Canadian Iroquois engine.
The Prime Minister has repeatedly urged the necessity for Canadian participation in U.S. armament production and this latter proposal would allow him to implement this policy as well as reactivate the Orenda and Avro plants at Malton.
This decision, based on the grounds of military effectiveness, of production sharing and of cost, has, we feel, unfortunately placed military considerations in an inferior position. And then the minister in reply to my assertion last evening that a smaller number of other types of aircraft would do the job of the F-104, said: Emphatically no; we need more aircraft for the strike role. In reply to that, if engines need replacing every 100 hours, half the aircraft will be in the hangars and not available when required. Canadian airmen like to fly; they like to get in enough practice to become efficient in the handling of their aircraft, and they are bound to put in these hours of practice regularly if they are to be able to fly their aircraft confidently at low altitudes and concentrate on the fire power that these planes carry. Surely, when this state of efficiency has to be attained you

Supply-National Defence cannot afford to have half your aircraft in the hangars. What good would they be, moreover, in the event of a sudden attack?
And so we were told this morning that as a result of prolonged examination the cabinet came to a conclusion and selected the F-104G; yet we have been told this afternoon that the F-104G has not been test flown or evaluated by the R.C.A.F. We have not been told, and I ask the minister this question, if the F-104G is a plane in being or whether it is just a plane on paper.
The minister told us that he was satisfied that the taxpayers' money was being spent properly. He went on to tell us that the F-104 had a very high performance and that it was a stable aircraft. Of course, it is a stable aircraft at high altitudes where it was designed to fly. Of course, it can do ordinary manoeuvres satisfactorily. But I asked the minister a few additional questions with reference to it. I asked him this morning what its maximum climbing incidence was and he said he could not tell me because the information is classified. I understand, however-and obviously I do not have this information from personal knowledge but from sources which I believe to be reliable -that if the F-104 has to climb too sharply the pilots cannot retain control of the aircraft. This characteristic is most essential in a strike reconnaissance plane. There are all sorts of possibilities where you have to have almost unlimited manoeuvreability and particularly the ability to make a very sharp ascent and reverse.
Let me read from Aircraft, Canada's aero trade magazine, issue of June, 1959, about another aircraft and how it works. This article is entitled "Thunderchief Testing", and reads as follows:
Officials have revealed that the Mach 2 Republic F-105 Thunderchief is completing 18 months of tests of a new bomb-releasing method. The tests, conducted at the U.S.A.F. Air Proving Ground Center Eglin AFB, Florida, ranged from tree-top level to 40,000 feet.
The new method is in answer to the problem of getting a bomb clear of a bomb bay when the vehicle is travelling at speeds up to Mach 2. At these speeds, if a bomb were merely released as was done in world war II bombers, the bomb would either be forced back up into the bomb bay or else would roll back along the underside of the fuselage doing damage to the aircraft structure.
To prevent this from happening, Republic has designed a pneumatic device which fires the bomb out with 30,000 pounds of force. To test the system initially, a special rig was constructed duplicating a full-scale bomb bay system. More than 100 "bombing runs" were made while elaborate electronic and recording equipment made minute evaluations of each ejection.
One of the features which I should have thought would be essential for strike reconnaissance is the ability of the plane to deliver
[Mr. Hellyer.j
satisfactorily a bomb load either of a conventional or nuclear type. It is obvious that when one of these bombs is being released, and particularly those of the nuclear variety, the pilot of the aircraft has to get his plane away from the scene very quickly in order to avoid being blown up with the explosion. This requires a very strategic manoeuvre and puts great stress on the aircraft. If the F-104 is not designed to do that and is not designed to be able to perform the skip bombing operation, it is not satisfactory for the R.C.A.F. as a strike reconnaissance plane.

The minister said this morning that R.C.A.F. pilots have flown the F-104 and that it was an easy transition from the F-86 to the F-104. It would be, of course, because they are similar aircraft. They are both day fighters designed for the same type of high level interception. We were told that we were taking advantage of the testing that had been done by others and that we would not have to do the development. Despite this, we were told just a few minutes ago that in fact the version the R.C.A.F. expects to buy has not been tested nor evaluated by us. Surely this means we will become involved in a period of redevelopment and redesign, a period of indecision in which we will not know for sure whether or not the new mark G will be a successful aircraft. In any event we on this side of the chamber believe that no redevelopment or redesign of that aircraft short of a complete redesign-in other words, a new aircraft- would fit it properly for the role of strike reconnaissance which the R.C.A.F. division overseas has now been assigned.
Supply-National Defence
In conclusion I wish to repeat what I have said before, that those of us who sit on this side of the chamber have a responsibility too. We are here to serve the Canadian public as are members on the government side. We try to do our job and our job is made more difficult by the fact that we do not have employees of the state to dig out facts and do our research for us. Consequently we have to work, as those of you who have sat on this side know, even more diligently than some members on the government side.
All the information we have been putting forward in respect of this plane has been put forward sincerely. It has not been the result of representations on behalf of anyone having anything to do directly or indirectly with the aircraft industry. Surely the minister could have shown us the consideration this morning of accepting as sincere the remarks that we put forward. When he was on this side of the house he put forward some very startling and peculiar ideas indeed and at that time we did not accuse him of being irresponsible. Irresponsible, Mr. Chairman? All I can say is that with respect to all the charges I put forward last night, namely that this aircraft was not designed for the strike role, that its engine is not satisfactory and that the casualty rate is high, the minister has shielded himself behind the veil of official secrecy while at the same time branding me by innuendo as being utterly irresponsible.
I feel that this is not fair and I know that on reflection the minister will realize that those of us on this side of the house have a responsibility to do our best to protect the taxpayers who elect us and to make sure that our fighting men overseas have the best equipment available from a military standpoint and that that consideration should be paramount unless there is some other very serious objection. We will continue to do this, and I assure the committee again that if we had felt this aircraft was a proper choice we would have applauded the government for making the decision, however tardy it was. However, I repeat, as I have said before, that we feel that the decision was ill-considered, that it was made hastily even though tardily just in time to have some bit of factual information to put before the committee when it began its deliberations on Thursday.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to repeat at any length the arguments already advanced by me in support of the decision reached by the government but there are one or two points which have arisen during the speeches made by the hon. member for Trinity. He is accusing the government of having made a hasty decision.

Supply-National Defence He says that nobody knew anything about the Lockheed or ever had any idea that we would consider the Lockheed aircraft until there was pressure put on the government or on the air force within the last month by a so-called high pressure advertising campaign. I should like to quote Hansard of March 2 when I made a speech on these matters. As found near the bottom of page 1515 I said:
Another problem we have before us is the possibility of having to replace the Sabres of our air division, the F-86.
Then I went on at some length to indicate some of the aircraft which were being inspected, and about half-way down the first column on page 1516 I used these words:
On the 14th and 16th of January yet another team went to the Lockheed aircraft company at Burbank, California.
I think that shows that this was not something which was suddenly thought up by the government in response to pressure exerted during the last month.
Then I must say just a word as to the engine, about which the hon. member has grave doubts. This is a comparatively new engine with high performance characteristics particularly well suited to the air division requirements. The engine is being installed in the new B-58 Hustler bomber, in the McDonnell F-4H all-weather interceptor and in the Convair 880 jet airliner and other new aircraft. I have no doubt at all of the excellence and reliability of this engine.
Reference was made to the fact that the engine has to be overhauled every 100 hours. That is a situation which applies to almost every new aircraft engine. By the time the engine is placed in the 104G's and made available to the R.C.A.F. I am assured that it will be able to run three or four times that many hours without being tested.
The only other point I want to refer to has to do with the conclusion the hon. member drew, and these were his words, that "military requirements held an inferior position to other considerations." I want to make it crystal clear that I deny that emphatically and I wish to say that the aircraft meets all the requirements which are laid down for the aircraft to carry out the role assigned to the squadrons in Europe.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has just told us that an air force team went to Burbank, California, in January of this year and that he had so advised the house on an earlier occasion. This is just one more instance of the minister taking things out of one context and putting them into an entirely different context. I remember very clearly this statement at the time we were criticizing the manner in which the CF-105 Avro Arrow

had been cancelled. The argument was not going as well for the government as it should have even though they had a lot of press clippings which supported them. The minister rose and in reply to a question as to what had been done to try to find work for the people at Avro and Orenda who had been thrown out of their jobs so abruptly he read off a list of about 20 different places that R.C.A.F. and other service teams had visited from time to time in the previous few months. He gave the impression at that time that these visits had been made for the purpose of trying to find something else of military value, before the cancellation of the Arrow was announced, which could be manufactured by the employees at Avro and Orenda. Yet in reply to a question which I put on the order paper the minister told the house that on not one occasion of these many was an employee, an executive or any other person representing Avro invited to go along in order that they might discuss with the officials of these various companies their capabilities and the things that they were best able to do.
It is completely obvious that these trips were not made for the specific purpose of trying to find something for the employees of Avro and Orenda to do before that abrupt cancellation was made and it is obvious today that this statement has been picked out of context to try to demonstrate that the government was then considering the Lockheed F-104 as a strike fighter when in fact the list he then read included a number of places which had not developed strike fighters and consideration was being given to planes and equipment of all types. Can you blame us, Mr. Chairman, for questioning the information which is given to us in the house and for demanding that we be given proper information and real facts on which to base our judgment before voting these huge amounts of money?

Mr. Chairman, I should like to stray a moment from the field of missiles, of plain or supersonic aircraft, to deal with a matter which is of particular interest, not only to my constituency of St. Jean, but also to the province of Quebec and to all of Canada, since it concerns the navy, the army and the air force, that is the Royal Military College of St. Jean.
I should like to draw the minister's attention to the fact that last year, on the occasion of this vote, I asked the minister if he could not find some way to let the Royal Military College of St. Jean give students there the opportunity of completing their course in St. Jean, instead of being forced to go to Kingston for that purpose.

I want to say to the minister that we, in St. Jean and in the province of Quebec in particular, are proud of the Royal Military College which with the Canadian military colleges of Kingston and Royal Roads has completed the trio of such institutions in Canada.
In 1952, the Liberal government gave the province of Quebec a bilingual royal military college, at the opening of which, in 1952, the commander at the time, Colonel Lahaie, who has earned quite a wide reputation in our province, stated that he hoped and that he was sure that five years after the opening of the college, that is in 1957, we could have in St. Jean a military college which would allow its students to take the same course as that given at Kingston.
Well, Mr. Chairman, this is 1959 and the Royal Military College of St. Jean still does not provide a complete course. I must say to the Minister of National Defence that, at the present time, I rise not only on behalf of the taxpayers, voters and citizens of the province of Quebec, but in my own name- and, since he is president of the Royal Military College, I am a little ill at ease in reminding him that he is the chairman of a college where students cannot take a course of studies or training.
Mr. Chairman, we have at the Royal Military College of St. Jean all the qualified staff we need to allow Canadians who attend the college to complete their course. I think it is unfair that French-speaking Canadians who start their training at the Royal Military College of St. Jean, and who stay on for three years, be forced, often after getting top marks among the cadets, to go to Kingston to complete their education in English. And there, quite often, because of their lack of knowledge of the English language, they fall to the bottom of the class of cadets who complete their studies at Kingston.
Mr. Chairman, since the Canadian government has provided a royal military college for the city of St. Jean, and the province of Quebec, I think this government must by all means enable students who attend this college to take their full training there.
May I point out to the Minister of National Defence the statement made in this house in 1952 as recorded on page 3941 of Hansard, by the Hon. Brooke Claxton, then Minister of National Defence, in which he indicated 66968-9-348
Supply-National Defence that the intention was to place the St. Jean military college on an equal footing with R.M.C. in Kingston.
Mr. Chairman, what is keeping this government from carrying out the intentions of the former government?
We have at St. Jean every facility to teach the full curriculum to our cadets. In the first place, we have a first rate president, in the person of the Minister of National Defence. We have an excellent commander, in the person of Group Captain Archambault, who is to be commended for doing an exceptionally fine job. We have, as director of studies, Colonel Charles A. Chabot, a man of outstanding reputation. We also have Squadron Leader Lanthier, a Kingston graduate, not to mention our devoted secretary general, Mr. Denis Dion, and all the distinguished professors devoted to the training of the cadets.
We have everything at St. Jean: a splendid site, the best of teachers and the best of college presidents. In fact, the only thing we lack is an opportunity for the cadets to complete their studies. I should be grateful, therefore, if the Minister of National Defence, who is president of our military college, would answer my request and tell us why we, in St. Jean, should not expect to see our royal military college at long last offer a complete course of studies, just as R.M.C. at Kingston.
I also ask the minister to tell us why Canadian citizens of French culture attending the royal military college at St. Jean are being forced to go to Kingston for the last two years of the course. Such students may find themselves at the bottom of the class when placed in an English environment, after leading their class at St. Jean.
When a bilingual military college was to be established at St. Jean, it was to be in the best interest of this country. I am convinced that the Minister of National Defence will not let this opportunity slip by to give the Royal Military College of St. Jean a complete study course so that the graduates of that college could be in the same category as the English speaking cadets in Kingston.
I shall not insist upon the matter, because I know how the Minister of National Defence is interested in anything having to do with the military college of St. Jean. I became aware of that interest during the visit he made there last year at the graduation ceremony. I also realized it this year when he came, accompanied by the hon. Solicitor
5488	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence General (Mr. Balcer), and if the teachers of that military college really have all the qualifications and abilities which the minister has recognized, we only need a quick decision by the minister. I would like us to be assured, as from next September, that those cadets who are now under the impression that they have to go to Kingston to complete their studies, will learn the great news that they will be able to continue their course in St. Jean, where they began their studies.
Before concluding these remarks, Mr. Chairman, I would like to add a few words. Quite recently, the minister informed me that it had been decided to demolish two buildings on the college grounds, which had been designated as surplus. At this stage, Mr. Chairman, I would like to point out to the minister that the two buildings he mentioned are historical sites in St. Jean. They are the remains of old Fort St. Jean and, to my mind, it would be in very bad taste to destroy them.
I am pleased to remind the house that the first fort at St. Jean was built in 1666; it was replaced by a second one in 1748, by a third in 1778 and by a fourth in 1839. The present fort, as well as the buildings which it is proposed to destroy, go back to 1839. I wanted to draw the minister's attention to that matter.
In my opinion, it would be unfortunate to demolish those historic buildings, even if it is proposed to replace them by more modern ones. Historic buildings going back to 1839 cannot, in my opinion, be replaced in 1959. It would be really unfortunate if the minister should decide to remove those buildings which have stood there for more than 120 years.
I know the minister will have a serious investigation made about the matter, and I can assure him that the great majority of the resident students of the Royal Military College of St. Jean, and of the people of St. Jean, that is 99 per cent of them, are opposed to the destruction of those buildings, as well as the whole population of the province of Quebec, and of Canada as a whole.
Mr. Chairman, I now close my remarks. However, I should like the Minister of National Defence to tell us why he has refused for so long to give the province of Quebec, and most particularly the Royal Military College of St. Jean, a course of study as complete as the one now being given at Kingston.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take the minister's mind back from the College St. Jean to the F-104. I do not


apologize to the committee for having something more to say about this matter, because, as has been pointed out, it represents a very large expenditure of the taxpayer's money, some $200 million or more; but more important than that, of course, is that it will be equipment for the R.C.A.F. in a new and difficult role which it may be asked to undertake for NATO and for Canada at a time when NATO tactics, and indeed NATO equipment, are in a state of flux. Therefore, we naturally on this side are worried about the implications of this decision. I would like to ask the minister one or two more questions, and I think they will be new questions. It is, of course, a fact-and I do not think the minister has disputed this -that the F-104 A, B, C, D, E, or F, has been developed in the United States as a high altitude, high speed aircraft. It has the world's speed record, and it was designed originally at least, the minister will agree I am sure, for a purpose not directly related to that which it will be performing with the R.C.A.F.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Not even indirectly related.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
If that is a fact, it was bound to arouse our anxiety and indeed our suspicion that this might not be the aircraft best equipped for the purpose we have in mind. We ask ourselves, how can this type of aircraft be suited for the strike fighter, strike reconnaissance role, at low altitudes, and the minister has replied that we are now considering the F-104G. The impression he has left in our minds is that this is a new model designed for this purpose to remove the deficiencies of the earlier models; but he has told us at the same time that this re-designed or this remodelled F-104F, the F-104G, has not been tested in the air by any Canadian pilot. Now, our worries about this plane have been increased by the evidence that we have been able to secure. Last night I asked the minister whether it was a fact that the United States-and this is a United States plane-has equipped its own tactical squadrons in Europe with Republic F-105 fighters, and the minister said in reply that some squadrons of the U.S.A.F. are being equipped with Republic F-105 planes. I would like to secure from him, if I can, information as to whether these replacements in Europe by the F-105 are replacements of the F-104.
The fact is, and the minister has not denied this, that the United States air force had already decided at the very time they were deciding to purchase these planes to reduce its own commitments for purchasing this plane from, I think, 700 to 300 or 400. This

is being done by the United States government, which should know a good deal about this plane, at a time also when it has signed new contracts, I think up until 1963, for the purchase of the F-105.
In connection with the testing of these planes, the minister said that the F-104G has not been tested in the air. I woud like to ask him whether the Grumman Super Tiger or the Republic F-105-I will just mention these two planes-has been tested or flown by the R.C.A.F.? When? For how many hours? Were they actually tested in the air in the form in which they were offered to the R.C.A.F., in the form in which they would be used by the R.C.A.F. if they had been purchased? In other words were those other types tested by the R.C.A.F.? Were they flown by the R.C.A.F.? When, and for how many hours?
I know there are economic considerations involved in this, Mr. Chairman, and the minister has indeed indicated that. I wonder whether he could give the committee any information about the unit prices for the F-104G. We remember in the debate on the CF-105, that in connection with prices we had a great deal of difficulty in getting the exact information on this point. The Prime Minister told us last February that the price of the CF-105, on an order of 100, was $7,810,000, and we learned from the Minister of Defence Production a couple of months later that, far from it being $7,810,000, it was $3,750,000. Perhaps the minister will give us some specific and definite information about the cost of these particular planes which it has been decided to buy from the United States.
I should also like to ask him whether any aviation company, apart from the Lockheed company, whose plane it has been decided to buy, whose planes were under consideration, including the Republic company, had expressed a willingness to use the Iroquois engine not only in their own aircraft for use in the R.C.A.F. but also for their own aircraft produced for use in the air force of the United States, because surely that would have been an important consideration in the mind of the government if in fact that proposal and that suggestion had been made.
Then I would also like to ask the minister whether this F-104G, this new model, improved version, which has not been tested by any Canadian flyer, has any all-weather or night flying capabilities?
When the question of the equipment of the United States air force was under discussion by the subcommittee of the committee on appropriations of the house of representatives this spring-and I am quoting 66968-9-348i
Supply-National Defence from page 536 of the evidence-the president of a company called Electronics Communications, Incorporated, who was a vicepresident of Westinghouse company before that, and who is a great expert in this field, was asked by the chairman of the committee: "What about the 104F?" They were discussing various types of planes, and Representative Flood went on to say, "Which has been slowed down, too"? He was referring to the cut in the order, and Mr. Godsey, who was the witness, said:
Sir, I have very little faith in a weapon or weapons system with limited capability. If you cannot use it at night or in bad weather then you have left yourself wide open to attack in those periods when you can do nothing.
Perhaps the minister will give us the information as to whether there is any allweather night flying capability of this model, the F-104G?
Then finally, at this stage, can the minister give us any indication of where this plane is to be manufactured in Canada and under what conditions? Supply-National Defence Roads, being English-speaking, are not up against the same language difficulties as the French-speaking students attending the St. Jean Royal Military College. The very aim of the Liberal party, in setting up a bilingual college, was to remedy this situation of inferiority in which Frenchspeaking students attending R.M.C. at Kingston found themselves.
I am sure that the minister understands my point perfectly. All that is found at St. Jean, but the minister persists in his refusal to authorize the Royal Military College of St. Jean to give those students an opportunity to complete their course in the same institution. I am proud that the powerful Minister of National Defence is head of that college. I trust he will reconsider the things I just said and that he will put an end to such discrimination against our people.

I am convinced that the Minister of National Defence very much appreciates what is done at St. Jean and that he likes to come and visit us. Mr. Chairman, I think we now have as clear a picture as we are likely to get of the role and activities of the R.C.A.F. I can only express my great anxiety over the decision which has been made to reequip our air division in Europe, a decision which has been made after a good deal of consideration no doubt by the government over many months, a decision which seems to have been based not on any actual flying test of the plane that has been picked by Canadian pilots, although there are a good many test pilots with a lot of experience who would have been available apart from the R.C.A.F., but based on considerations which do not require, so the minister says, that kind of test.
Anyway, the minister says that the decision has been made and we must all hope that this particular plane, whatever doubts we may have about its suitability for this role, will turn out to be a suitable plane for the important and responsible new role that the R.C.A.F. is being asked to perform in Europe. I take it that it will not begin the performance of that role for a good many months because the minister has said it will be about 18 months before the first planes are delivered to the squadrons in Europe. Presumably during that period of 18 months or more these squadrons will continue to carry on as efficiently as they always do, with the F-86.
In the future, however, they will have a new function to perform while, on the other hand, the CF-100 squadron will carry on, the minister has said, the function which they have been performing over the years in Europe with efficiency and distinction, as a result of which the Canadian air division, I think, now has the reputation in the NATO forces of being as efficient, as effective and as well trained as any air unit in all of the NATO forces. Nevertheless, it must be quite clear to everyone that the CF-100, while not entirely obsolescent, is becoming less effective as the months go by in the face of the air menace which the NATO forces will have to counter in Europe if there ever is an outbreak of war.

Then, Mr. Chairman, there will be the nine CF-100 squadrons in Canada integrated into the North American air defence command and playing their part as manned interceptors with United States squadrons under NORAD which are or will soon be equipped with planes more modern and more effective than the CF-100 is at the present time. I have already stated my view that the government should be giving a most searching examination to the possibility of a new role for the R.C.A.F. on this continent. It has been suggested in some press quarters that in making the proposal to the government for this kind of re-examination I have been advocating the drastic reduction of the R.C.A.F. The minister will know that it not what I said, even in the question which I asked him. What I do advocate is an examination in order to see if there should not be a drastic reorientation or reorganization of the role of the R.C.A.F. in the defence of Canada, in the defence of the alliance and in the defence of peace.
I have no illusion about the importance of the R.C.A.F. in any form of defence because it is bound to be of the very greatest importance and I think it would be very silly on the part of anyone who believes in collective defence, who believes, as I do, in Canada playing its full part in collective defence and paying its full share of the collective insurance premium, to think that the R.C.A.F. will not have a very important role to perform. But I have suggested that perhaps that role, under new conditions, will have to be altered in the future and that perhaps there are other ways in which the R.C.A.F. could operate effectively, and perhaps in a more Canadian way. I mentioned that we could make our armed units more mobile and air-transportable, but that this would take a good deal of reorganization of the R.C.A.F.
The minister replied to that suggestion yesterday by saying he felt that it would be unwise at this time to use the resources of the R.C.A.F. for that particular purpose, beyond that which it performs now. I am not an expert in tactics or strategy, and if that is the considered view of the minister and his advisers that it would be unwise to make that change at this time, that is how it has to stand. But I do believe that this particular role of continental air defence, operated as it is being operated now by CF-lOO's, is going to make a less and less important contribution to collective defence in the months and years to come. I do not see how, if we are going to continue to play that role, we can avoid the decision of reequipping the nine Canadian squadrons of the R.C.A.F. in Canada, because the minister 66968-9-349
Supply-National Defence has confirmed the information we have received from many other quarters that in the course of time the bomber will be less and less effective and the missile will be more and more effective. None of these aircraft, even the F-108 which may be in operation a few years from now, will be of the slightest use against missiles. This being the case, perhaps we should be looking ahead for a new role for the R.C.A.F. in common defence.
This was all I had in mind when I mentioned this matter. I have expressed the hope that the government would give that kind of re-examination of defence policy and defence planning, and not prolong indefinitely the kind of operation which has been performed with distinction and efficiency by the R.C.A.F. in the past, but which may not be a realistic participation in Atlantic defence much longer. I would have thought, I thought and I still think, that if we could have had a committee to go into this whole question of the role, not only of the R.C.A.F. but the other armed forces in the common defence, to which we could have called witnesses, we would have been in a better position to make the right kind of defence decisions in this parliament than we are now. I think we have had a vindication of that view this afternoon in the kind of discussion we have had about the $200 million to be expended for airplanes for the air division overseas.
However, Mr. Chairman, I am quite sure that whatever role the government may give the R.C.A.F., whether or not it is the most effective role in the present circumstances -and we have some doubts about that-it is bound to be an important role and it is bound to be carried out with efficiency and devotion.
