subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
I suppose this is the item upon which we ask any questions we may have to ask on the early warning systems. I should like to ask the minister one or two questions on this very important part of our continental defence system, because however we may feel about the relative importance of continental defence as a protection for communities and areas, and as a protection of the bases from which the deterrent can operate, the fact remains that either of these two aspects of continental defence will be ineffective unless we have an efficient early warning system. This has been the reason for spending the millions and millions of dollars that have been spent by both countries on the three lines, the Distant Early Warning line, the Pinetree line and the Mid-Canada line, the expense of which has been shared between the two countries.
We know now that while these lines are, I think, reasonably effective in giving warning of an attack by bomber aircraft-reasonably effective because it is idle to think they will ever be 100 per cent effective, they are mechanical after all-which was the original purpose otherwise they would not have been


built, they are not of any value at all in respect of giving warning against attack by intercontinental ballistic missiles. The government of the United States, therefore, proposes to spend billions of dollars on a ballistic missile early warning system, in spite of the fact that growing bodies of expert and political opinion in the United States are questioning the wisdom of these astronomical expenditures. Even if they are successful, they will only give about 15 minutes, though that 15 minutes may be very important. I gathered from the minister's remarks yesterday and the day before that Canada is not going to participate directly in these expenditures, and I think if that is the decision it is a very wise decision. We do not know where it is going to lead us in terms of expenditure and in terms of mechanical results.
However, I am worried also about a growing body of technical criticism against the effectiveness of this whole continental effort, because it is continental, whether we participate in it in one form or another. As I mentioned in the statement I made the other day, criticism has been made of this effort by a man who, the minister will agree, is as great an expert in the field of radar as anyone alive, namely Sir Robert Watson-Watt, who is the man perhaps as responsible for the victory in the Battle of Britain as any other single individual because of what he did in the 1930's to make radar detection possible. He has been saying in the United States and in Canada that we are wasting our money and wasting our effort in attempting to secure an early warning system that will be effective in any real sense against the new methods of attack. He is quoted in the press of May 27, 1959 as saying:
-that the present radar defence system is "far advanced toward obsolescence". The British radar expert also contended in this article that the new extension of the DEW line, the ballistic missile early warning system (BMEWS) which uses three stations each with a five thousand mile radar sweep to give a 15-minute warning against ballistic missiles, is "at best, a very expensive way to get a still inadequate warning".
I wonder whether the minister can give us some information which will be a little more reassuring as to the value and effectiveness of all the work that has gone on and is likely to go on in this vitally important field of early warning.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
I agree with the Leader of the Opposition that this is a vitally important field, and we must endeavour to obtain those early warnings both for the protection of our own people and for the protection of the retaliatory forces in the United States.
The DEW line and the other systems were never designed to be effective against a missile; they were designed to be effective

against the bomber. Innumerable tests have been carried out on these lines and they have proved extraordinarily effective in locating the type of target which we believe the Russians would be able to use against this continent in the form of manned bombers. Improvements have been and are continually being made in the actual instruments which are being used on the DEW line. The DEW line has been extended out into the ocean now linking up with the similar warning systems in Europe. I think I can say definitely that a very high degree of reliability can be placed in our DEW line and warning system in giving information about the approach of hostile bombers.
With regard to detection stations which are being erected by the United States-not in Canada-Canada is not making any direct contributions toward those. We are having research work done in order to detect objects which are in the atmosphere, and the results of the experiments and research work which are carried out are passed on to the United States; but there is no direct expenditure in these estimates toward the construction or the maintenance of the BMEWS systems.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
I am glad to get that information from the minister, but, it is reassuring only to the point where it confirms that we shall have some warning against bombers if they ever were loosed against this continent; perhaps enough warning to scatter to the hills. But against missiles, in spite of all the work that may be done in the future, the best we can really hope for is about 15 minutes. That will mean much from the point of view of getting a retaliatory force into the air. It will not give much comfort to the 200 million people on this continent that they have 15 minutes to escape destruction and grope for survival while the retaliatory force is on the way to the enemy and putting the 200 million people in that country in the same position. That is about the best we can hope for if we ever allow this sort of thing to happen.
Can the minister give us some information about the actual administration and operation of the DEW line? He said that it is now under the operational control of the R.C.A.F. Can he tell us how many R.C.A.F. officers there are in the DEW line and what they are controlling? It has been suggested-among others, by the Prime Minister-that the situation in the DEW line in regard to protection of Canadian sovereignty is much better than it was a couple of years ago. Has the minister any information on this point? It is my own view, and it is confirmed by the information I have been able to receive in answers to questions on the orders of the 66968-9-349J
Supply-National Defence day, that there is no change whatever in the last two and a half years in the legal and jurisdictional position of control of the DEW line, and that the rights of sovereignty which were reserved for Canada in the original agreement-and they are there in black and white-have been sufficient during the years to ensure that our sovereignty is respected. Perhaps the minister can give me some information about operational control of the DEW line.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: There are four main centres in Canada of the DEW line as well as a number of satellite installations to those four centres. Satellite installations are mainly automatic. The information obtained either from the main station or from the satellite stations is filtered through into an operational room at these four main centres. Until January 1 of this year the United States air force officers had the operational control of those control rooms; they were in charge of those rooms. As the information came in, it was filtered through to them, and they made the decision as to what information would be passed back to NORAD or to the air defence command of Canada. Since January 1 the R.C.A.F. officers have taken over those control rooms, and there is a United States liaison officer only at the control rooms. Our sovereignty is respected in full in those Arctic stations.

three main reasons why there is a considerable reduction. First of all, the forces of our European allies are being built up and are being equipped by their own efforts, and are in a better state of preparedness than they were a few years ago.

I am sure that as a member of the previous administration the hon. Leader of the Opposition is very familiar with the purpose of these dollar items. The reason is that it is a commitment authority, and in defence planning the construction of new equipment, be it aircraft, ships, guns, or the building of certain projects, has to be projected for two, three, four or more years, and one cannot really embark on this general program unless there is some assurance given that under normal circumstances it will be continued.
I might say that the purpose of this vote is to authorize the same system of administrative commitment as in previous years, and it has been going on now for a good many
Supply-National Defence years. In the past this has been done by the wording of a single defence vote, but now that these estimates have been divided up on the recommendation of the parliamentary committee another procedure has to be adopted. The same policy is now being accomplished by this special item, the effect of which is to put a limit on the total commitments that may be entered into without certifying, in accordance with section 30 of the Financial Administration Act, that funds are available to meet those commitments. With the increasing number of items which require to be dealt with, this system of certification has proved to be somewhat cumbersome and unsatisfactory.

speechtext:
The minister has explained that this item is the authority to make commitments for expenditures in the future. What concerns me, in the light of that explanation, is how he justifies the expenditure under item 222 which is an item for the acquisition of major equipment-the part that is relevant. How can he justify using funds voted by parliament under the designation "acquisition of major equipment" for the termination of the Arrow contract? speechtext: Perhaps there is no point in my pursuing the matter further. subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
I should like to ask the minister if he prefers this new method of putting these votes into the estimates and whether he has any comment to make on the possibility that by dividing them between the three services might accentuate the rivalry between the different branches of the armed forces. I know that we in Canada have been most fortunate in that there has been a very co-operative attitude between chiefs of staff, who have considered themselves to be representative of the Canadian armed services as a whole as well as being representative of their own services.
Does the minister think there is any possibility that adopting this new method of putting these votes into the estimates will tend to reduce this co-operative attitude or to encourage in any way a struggle within the Canadian armed forces to obtain a larger proportion of the total appropriation in any particular vote? I know this is a real problem. Under the old system we had flexibility, and the ability to transfer money from


one service to the other if the need of any one service became more urgent in the course of a year. I hope we will not emulate Washington in this regard and I hope the new system will not encourage any rivalry whatsoever, but that whatever system we do adopt finally will be the one most likely to further the conception of a unified Canadian defence force.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: I am sure this will not cause any rivalry between the forces. The forces knew exactly, before, how much money would be available to them. What this will do is to give parliament a tighter control over expenditure and it will improve the administration in the forces because no longer will there be any pool of money left over at the end which could be easily transferred from one force to another. It will mean that much better estimating will be done at the beginning by the various forces. I should like to commend the committee on its recommendation, which I welcome in this respect, and that is why it has been introduced.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: I was merely putting my comment forward as a question, and if the minister is satisfied I think we can accept his assurances on this point.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this item covers rifle associations, military service associations, military united service institutes and others. subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
There have been no additions made to the grants in these estimates. In fact, most of the grants to these various organizations have been the same for a great many years. All of these associations have to report their financial standing to national defence headquarters at the end of each year. They are checked regarding their particular activity not only by national defence headquarters but by the various commands in which they are situated.
With respect to associations as rifle associations, I think it quite obvious what their objectives are. As far as service associations are concerned they are groups of representatives from all parts of Canada for the particular arm of the service or the particular

force. They meet together periodically and submit recommendations representing, let us say, the militia, or the infantry of the militia or the artillery or the air cadets, whatever the case may be.
The grants to the service institutions are grants which are made to enable those clubs consisting of retired and serving officers, both in the regular and auxiliary and reserve forces, to keep in touch with military developments by means of holding periodical lectures and by inviting distinguished visitors they may like to invite to speak to them on military matters. There is no change in that.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: They all report annually to your department and so you know they are functioning properly?

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH ORDERS OF THE HOUSE

speechtext: My question is somewhat similar to that of the hon. member for Kootenay West. I am thinking of grants to the united services institutes. The amount of the grants vary. Do these vary in accordance with a fixed scale of contribution based on paid up membership?

subtopic: PRESENTATION OF REGIMENTAL COLOURS
PRESENTATION OF REGIMENTAL COLOURS
speechtext:
1.	Will Her Majesty, Queen Elizabeth, present regimental colours to the Canadian army unit formerly known as the Cape Breton highlanders, during her coming visit to Canada?
2.	If so, where and when will this presentation be made?
Answer by: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker
(Prime Minister):
1 and 2. When the itinerary for Her Majesty was drawn up it was realized that there would not be time in many places to carry out the functions and ceremonies requested by many civilian and service agencies and units. Some 10 or more regiments requested the honour of presentation of colours by Her Majesty.
During the royal visit to South Africa of His Majesty King George V a precedent had been set by the presentation of colours to several regiments at one parade. This year several regiments were asked to participate by sending colour parties to certain localities where time and the program for Her Majesty permitted the presentation ceremony to be conducted. One of these occasions was the presentation held on parliament hill on July 1.
In the case of the second battalion Nova Scotia highlanders (Cape Breton) the regiment was asked to send a colour party to one of the localities where presentation was to be made and the offer was declined because they wished to have the ceremony take place when all ranks and relatives could be present.
On the authority of His Excellency the Governor General the Lieutenant-Governor of Nova Scotia, General B. C. Plow, presented colours to the regiment. A special message from Her Majesty was sent from Buckingham Palace to be read at the parade.
